title: What Should an Agent Forget? Separating What Is Stored from What Is Used
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 9 Sep 2026]
    Title:What Should an Agent Forget? Separating What Is Stored from What Is Used
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Persistent language agents need stored experience to remain available across time, while each answer requires evidence suited to a particular question. A superseded fact can mislead a current-state answer and still be essential for a historical query. We present RD-Forget, a training-free framework that separates what an agent stores from what it uses. A retained source archive preserves observations, and a query-conditioned memory view controls their influence on the current answer. A frozen language-model curator extracts relevant evidence, groups facts into semantic slots, and preserves the relations needed for multi-hop reasoning. Same-slot replacement links suppress superseded values in current-state contexts, while intent-aware retrieval makes earlier evidence eligible again. A rate-distortion formulation guides construction of the answer-time view within a memory budget. Experiments span conversational memory, knowledge updating, fact consolidation, long-context reasoning, and personalization under a shared answering pipeline. The results associate accurate answers with both query-relevant evidence construction and control over obsolete alternatives. Configurations without forgetting or query conditioning have the largest score deficits, while slot grouping, historical access, and relation preservation contribute complementary functions. Retaining history while selectively controlling its use offers a practical way to accommodate changing facts and future questions.

report.summary: RD-Forget, a training-free framework, separates an agent's stored memory from the query-conditioned evidence it uses, helping current answers ignore superseded facts while retaining history.
report.background: Persistent language agents are increasingly expected to remember users, tasks, and changing facts across sessions. Most memory systems either retain everything in a vector store or overwrite old entries when new facts arrive. Both approaches fail in common cases: a stale address can corrupt a current-state answer, yet deleting it breaks historical queries. Long-context models and retrieval-augmented generation help, but they do not explicitly decide which remembered evidence should influence a specific answer. Existing knowledge-editing and memory-consolidation methods often require training or destructive updates. RD-Forget enters this gap by treating memory as two layers: a durable archive of observations and a query-conditioned view assembled at answer time.
key_points: RD-Forget separates storage from use. The agent keeps a full source archive of past observations, but a query-conditioned memory view decides which evidence reaches the current answer. The framework is training-free, so it can sit on top of existing language models rather than requiring fine-tuning or a new model architecture.

A frozen language-model curator extracts relevant evidence, groups facts into semantic slots, and preserves relations needed for multi-hop reasoning. Same-slot replacement links mark superseded values so they are suppressed in current-state contexts, while intent-aware retrieval can make older evidence eligible again for historical questions.

The answer-time view is built under a memory budget using a rate-distortion formulation. This means the system explicitly trades off compression and relevance, selecting a compact evidence set that should answer the query well while omitting distracting or obsolete alternatives.

Experiments cover conversational memory, knowledge updating, fact consolidation, long-context reasoning, and personalization under a shared answering pipeline. Results associate accurate answers with both query-relevant evidence construction and control over obsolete alternatives. Configurations without forgetting or query conditioning show the largest score deficits, while slot grouping, historical access, and relation preservation add complementary benefits.

The work reframes forgetting as selective use, not deletion. Agents can retain history for auditability, personalization, and future historical queries, while preventing outdated facts from hijacking current-state answers. This shifts memory management from a storage problem toward an access-policy problem.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the paper pushes agent memory beyond simple vector retrieval or destructive knowledge editing. It suggests memory quality will be judged by query-conditioned control, not just recall volume, which could influence RAG pipelines, evaluation benchmarks, and enterprise knowledge assistants. Developers gain a blueprint that is training-free and model-agnostic, potentially easier to test in production than fine-tuned memory policies; memory stores, graph databases, and retrieval layers may need to expose slots, relations, and versioning. Regular users could see assistants that remember preferences and past conversations but stop repeating expired details, while still answering “what did I say before?” Privacy and compliance teams may welcome retained history with controlled use, though it also raises governance questions about what is stored and for how long.
report.tools: RD-Forget has no public code in the abstract, so start by watching its arXiv page. Related open-source projects to explore: Letta/MemGPT and Mem0 for agent memory; Zep/Graphiti for temporal knowledge graphs; LangGraph or LlamaIndex for query-conditioned retrieval pipelines; Qdrant, Chroma, or Weaviate for vector storage with metadata. These can prototype slot grouping, versioning, and historical access before RD-Forget code appears.
